title: War, Mail and Crossing Oceans
summary: When war came in 1914, airplanes quickly changed from fragile scouts into fighting machines, and factories built them by the thousands. After the war, brave pilots carried the mail through the night and flew across the stormy Atlantic. Heroes like Alcock and Brown, Bessie Coleman, Charles Lindbergh and Amelia Earhart showed the world what airplanes could do.

sections.heading: From Eyes in the Sky to Guns in the Sky
paragraphs: In August 1914, only about eleven years after the Wright brothers' twelve-second hop at Kill Devil Hills, the great powers of Europe went to war. The airplanes they took with them were still flimsy things of wood, wire and fabric. Germany had a paper strength of about 230 army airplanes, but only around 180 of them were fit to fly. Britain sent just a few squadrons to France, with about 30 machines that actually worked. Most generals thought of airplanes as interesting toys, useful perhaps for looking around, but not much more.

Looking around, it turned out, was hugely important. For centuries, armies had sent horse riders called cavalry ahead to spot the enemy. But in the summer of 1914 the armies were enormous and moved fast, and a pilot a thousand metres up could see more in an hour than a cavalry patrol could see in a day. On 22 August 1914, British airmen spotted German troops under General von Kluck moving in a way that threatened to surround the British army near the Belgian town of Mons. Their reports helped the British pull back in time. Suddenly, nobody laughed at the flying machines anymore.

Soon the war settled into long lines of muddy trenches stretching across France and Belgium. Airplanes became the army's eyes. Two-seater planes carried an observer with a camera that took pictures on glass plates, because the film of the time was not sharp enough. Back on the ground, photographers pieced hundreds of these pictures together like a jigsaw puzzle to make detailed maps of the enemy's trenches. Other planes helped artillery gunners hit targets they could not see. By March 1915 some observation planes carried a Morse-code radio transmitter, though not a receiver, so the gunners on the ground answered by laying out strips of white cloth in patterns the pilot could read from above.

If your enemy has eyes in the sky, the obvious next step is to try to poke them out. At first pilots and observers shot at each other with pistols and rifles, and some even threw bricks or dragged hooks on ropes. Mounting a machine gun was the obvious answer, but there was a tricky problem. On most planes the propeller was at the front, spinning more than a thousand times a minute. A pilot naturally wanted to aim his gun by pointing the whole airplane at the target, which meant firing straight forward. But firing straight forward meant shooting through your own propeller.

sections.heading: The Gun That Fired Between the Blades
paragraphs: The first bold solution came from the French pilot Roland Garros, who before the war had been famous for flying across the Mediterranean Sea. By March 1915 his Morane-Saulnier Type L monoplane had wedge-shaped steel plates bolted onto the back of each propeller blade. Most bullets passed between the blades, and the few that would have hit a blade bounced off the steel wedges instead. It was crude and it put extra strain on the engine, but it worked well enough for Garros to shoot down German planes in April 1915. Then, on 18 April, he was forced to land behind German lines and was captured. He tried to burn his plane, but the propeller survived well enough for the Germans to study his strange armoured design.

They asked the young Dutch aircraft maker Anthony Fokker, who was building planes for Germany, to look into it. Fokker's team, including the engineer Heinrich Lübbe, came up with something cleverer: a synchronization gear. The word synchronize means to make two things happen in time with each other. Here is how it worked. A cam, which is a small bump on a spinning shaft, was turned by the engine itself. Once every turn of the propeller, the cam pushed a rod or linkage that let the gun fire a single shot, timed so that the bullet passed through the gap while the blades were out of the way. The engine and the gun were, in a sense, dancing to the same beat. A popular story says Fokker invented it in just 48 hours, but historians now doubt that, and the idea itself was not entirely new: the Swiss engineer Franz Schneider and the Frenchman Raymond Saulnier had both designed similar gears before the war. Fokker's team was the first to make one that worked reliably in battle.

The gear was fitted to the Fokker E.I, a small single-seat monoplane called the Eindecker, meaning one-wing. The first victory by a plane with a synchronized gun is believed to have come on 1 July 1915. For several months German pilots held an advantage that British newspapers nicknamed the Fokker Scourge. But the basic idea could not stay secret for long, and by the middle of 1916 Britain and France had their own synchronizers in large numbers. This back-and-forth would repeat again and again for the rest of the war: one side built a better plane, then the other side caught up.

It is important to remember that behind the newspaper headlines about daring air duels, this was a terrible time. Pilots who shot down five or more enemy planes were called aces, and by the end of the war there were more than 1,800 of them. But many young airmen, often only 19 or 20 years old, did not survive. In April 1917, the worst month of the war for Britain's Royal Flying Corps, a British pilot at the front could expect, on average, to survive only about 93 hours of flying. Many others died in training accidents before they ever reached the front. Airships called Zeppelins, and later big Gotha bomber planes, dropped bombs on English towns and London, killing hundreds of ordinary people. The airplane, the dream of so many peaceful inventors, had become a weapon.

sections.heading: Factories, Pilots and a Sheet-Metal Donkey
paragraphs: War is cruel, but it also pours money and people into technology at an astonishing speed. In 1914, airplanes were built in small workshops, often one at a time. By 1918, France and Britain were each turning out tens of thousands of airplanes, and Germany, Italy and later the United States were building them by the thousands too. Engines became far more powerful and reliable. Factories learned to make identical parts, so a broken plane could be fixed with spares. Tens of thousands of people learned to fly, and many more learned to build, repair and design airplanes. In April 1918, Britain combined its army and navy flying services into a brand-new Royal Air Force, the first air force in the world that was independent of an army or a navy.

Most planes of the war were still biplanes made of wooden frames covered in fabric and braced with wires. But one German engineer was already thinking much further ahead. Hugo Junkers was a professor and businessman in his fifties who had made a fortune designing gas water heaters. He believed that the future of flying belonged to airplanes made entirely of metal, with thick wings strong enough to hold themselves up without any outside struts or wires. Engineers call this a cantilever wing, the same idea as a diving board that sticks out from one end with no support at the other.

His first all-metal plane, the Junkers J 1, was built in 1915. Aluminium was rare and expensive, so Junkers used thin sheets of steel, the kind normally used in electrical equipment. Steel is heavy, and the J 1 earned the affectionate nickname Blechesel, German for Tin Donkey or Sheet-Metal Donkey. On 12 December 1915, Leutnant Theodor Mallinckrodt took it on a first short hop that reached a height of almost 3 metres, and in January 1916 it made proper flights at Döberitz near Berlin. Powered by a 120-horsepower Mercedes engine, it could reach about 170 km/h, which was fast for its day, thanks to its smooth, clean shape with no drag-producing wires.

The Tin Donkey never went into battle; it was too heavy and climbed too slowly. But it proved a point that would shape every airliner you have ever seen: a metal airplane with an unbraced wing could fly, and fly well. Later Junkers designs switched to lighter aluminium alloys, and after the war his company built the F 13, one of the first all-metal airliners. The J 1 itself was put on display in the Deutsches Museum in Munich in 1926, but sadly it was destroyed in a bombing raid during the next world war, in December 1944.

When the fighting finally ended on 11 November 1918, the world was left with thousands of surplus airplanes, thousands of trained pilots, and a big question: what could flying machines do in peacetime?

sections.heading: The Mail Must Get Through
paragraphs: One answer arrived in an envelope. On 15 May 1918, while the war in Europe was still going on, the United States started its first regular air mail route, linking Washington, D.C., Philadelphia and New York. The planes were Curtiss JN-4 biplanes, nicknamed Jennies, the same kind used to train army pilots. Sending a letter by air cost 24 cents, which was a lot of money at the time, and the Post Office printed a special red and blue 24-cent stamp showing a Jenny. Because the stamp went through the printing press twice, once for each colour, one sheet of 100 stamps was printed with the airplane upside down. A stamp collector bought that sheet at a post office counter for its normal price. Today a single Inverted Jenny is one of the most valuable stamps in the world; one sold in 2023 for about two million dollars.

At first the army flew the mail, then the Post Office took over with its own pilots. The bold dream was a route right across the country, from New York to San Francisco. But early planes could only fly safely in daylight, so at night the mail bags were loaded onto trains, which wiped out much of the time saved by flying. Members of Congress began to wonder whether air mail was worth the money at all.

The answer came in a dramatic winter dash on 22 and 23 February 1921. The Post Office set out to prove that mail could be flown coast to coast day and night. Several pilots took part in relays, but snowstorms grounded many of them. A pilot named Jack Knight was supposed to fly only one leg, but when his replacement could not get through, he kept going, flying through the dark and the snow from North Platte, Nebraska, toward Chicago, a distance of about 1,300 kilometres. He had a broken nose from an earlier crash, a simple compass and a torn road map. On the ground, postal workers, airfield staff and farmers lit bonfires to mark the way. Knight landed in Chicago at 8:40 in the morning, and the mail crossed the whole country in about 33 hours and 20 minutes. His flight made front-page news and helped convince Congress to keep paying for air mail.

Bonfires were not a long-term plan. Starting in 1923 the government built something new: a lighted airway, a road in the sky made of light. Steel towers about 16 metres tall were set up roughly every 16 kilometres, and each one carried a powerful rotating beacon that swept the sky six times a minute. On the ground beside many towers lay a huge concrete arrow, painted bright yellow, pointing toward the next beacon. Pilots flying at night simply hopped from one flashing light to the next, like following a trail of glowing breadcrumbs. Night air mail flights began on 1 July 1924, and by June 1925 the lit airway stretched about 4,300 kilometres from New York to San Francisco.

Flying the mail was dangerous work. In the early years many air mail pilots were killed in crashes caused by bad weather, fog and engine failure. But their flights showed that airplanes could keep a schedule, and in 1925 a new law let private companies bid to carry the mail. Some of those small mail companies would grow into the big airlines you will meet in Part 14.

sections.heading: Fog, Ice and a Bog: Alcock and Brown
paragraphs: Even before the war ended, a British newspaper, the Daily Mail, had offered a prize of 10,000 pounds, a fortune at the time, for the first airplane to fly across the Atlantic Ocean nonstop. In spring 1919, several teams gathered in Newfoundland, the closest point in North America to Europe, with their machines packed in crates.

One team was two Royal Air Force veterans. John Alcock, the pilot, was a 26-year-old from Manchester who had been fascinated by engines since boyhood. Arthur Whitten Brown, the navigator, was an engineer born in Glasgow to American parents. Both had been prisoners of war. Their airplane was a Vickers Vimy, a big biplane bomber designed for the war, with two 360-horsepower Rolls-Royce Eagle engines. Its bomb racks had been removed and replaced with extra fuel tanks holding about 865 gallons of petrol.

At about 1:45 in the afternoon on 14 June 1919, the heavily loaded Vimy lumbered off a field near St. John's, barely clearing the trees. Almost everything that could go wrong did. The little wind-driven generator failed, which meant no radio, no intercom and no heating in their open cockpit. An exhaust pipe split, so the engine roared deafeningly beside them all night. Thick fog and cloud hid the sea, the sky and the stars, and Brown needed to see the Sun or stars to work out their position with his sextant, an instrument for measuring angles. Twice, flying blind in cloud, Alcock lost control and the plane spiralled down until the fog cleared just above the waves. Around 3 a.m. they flew into a snowstorm, and ice built up on the plane and its engines. A famous story says Brown climbed out onto the wings in the freezing dark to chip ice off the engines, but Brown himself never described doing this, so it is probably a legend.

At about 8:40 the next morning, 15 June, they spotted the coast of Ireland and landed near the town of Clifden in County Galway on what looked like a lovely green field. It turned out to be Derrigimlagh Bog, and the Vimy's wheels sank into the soft ground and tipped the plane onto its nose. Neither man was hurt. They had flown about 3,040 kilometres in just under 16 hours, the first nonstop flight across the Atlantic.

Winston Churchill, then the minister in charge of the air force, presented their prize, and within about a week King George V knighted both men. Sadly, Sir John Alcock died in a crash in France just six months later, in December 1919. Their Atlantic crossing was a triumph, but it also showed how risky long flights still were. To be fair to everyone, they were not the only ocean-crossers that year. A few weeks earlier, in May 1919, a US Navy flying boat called the NC-4 had crossed the Atlantic in stages, stopping in the Azores islands along the way, and in July the British airship R34 crossed in both directions. Alcock and Brown's claim to fame is that they did it in one nonstop hop, so 1919 became the year the Atlantic was first conquered by air.

sections.heading: Queen Bess: Bessie Coleman Learns in French
paragraphs: Bessie Coleman was born on 26 January 1892 in Atlanta, Texas, the tenth of thirteen children. Her mother was African American and her father may have had Cherokee or Choctaw grandparents. The family were sharecroppers, poor farmers who worked someone else's land, and as a girl Bessie picked cotton and walked kilometres to a one-room school. She loved maths and books, saved her money, and later moved to Chicago, where she worked as a manicurist in a barbershop.

In the barbershop she heard soldiers home from the war telling stories about flying in France. She decided she would fly too. There was one enormous problem: in the United States at that time, no flight school would accept a student who was a woman, and none would accept a student who was Black. Bessie was both. Robert Abbott, the publisher of the Chicago Defender, an important Black newspaper, told her to try France instead, where attitudes were different. She took French lessons at night, and with help from Abbott and a Chicago banker named Jesse Binga, she sailed for Paris on 20 November 1920.

In France she learned to fly a Nieuport biplane. On 15 June 1921 the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale, the international organization that issues pilot licences and records, gave her a licence. She was the first African American woman, and the first woman of Native American descent, to earn a pilot's licence.

Back in America, Coleman became a barnstormer, a stunt pilot who toured the country performing at air shows. Crowds called her Queen Bess. She did loops and figure eights and walked on wings, and she used her fame for a purpose. She refused to perform at shows where Black spectators were not allowed in, or had to use separate gates, and she dreamed of opening a flying school so that other Black Americans would not face the barriers she had. She never got the chance. On 30 April 1926, while preparing for a show in Jacksonville, Florida, her plane went into a dive and she was thrown out and killed, along with her mechanic, William Wills. Investigators later found that a loose wrench had jammed the controls. She was only 34. Her dream did not die with her: within a few years, a flying club named after Bessie Coleman was helping Black Americans learn to fly in Los Angeles, and today every year pilots drop flowers over her grave in Chicago.

sections.heading: Lucky Lindy and the Spirit of St. Louis
paragraphs: In 1919 a New York hotel owner named Raymond Orteig, who had been born in France, offered a 25,000-dollar prize for the first nonstop flight between New York and Paris. That is about 5,800 kilometres, nearly twice as far as Alcock and Brown had flown. For years nobody could do it. Several famous pilots tried in big planes with multiple engines and crews, and some of them crashed or vanished.

Charles Lindbergh was a tall, quiet 25-year-old from Minnesota. He had been a barnstormer and an army-trained pilot, and since 1926 he had flown the air mail between St. Louis and Chicago, often at night and in bad weather. He believed the best way to win was the opposite of what everyone else was trying: one engine, one pilot, and as much fuel as possible. With money from St. Louis businessmen and his own air mail savings, he ordered a plane from the small Ryan Airline Company in San Diego. In about 60 days, Lindbergh and Ryan's engineer Donald Hall turned their design into the Spirit of St. Louis.

The Spirit was really a flying fuel tank. It had a single 223-horsepower Wright Whirlwind radial engine, and its wing was stretched to 14 metres to lift about 450 US gallons of fuel. The main fuel tank sat in front of the pilot for safety, so there was no front windshield at all; Lindbergh looked ahead through side windows or a small periscope. To save weight he left behind a radio, a parachute and even a proper seat cushion, using a wicker chair. He navigated by dead reckoning, which means working out your position from your speed, compass heading and the time that has passed.

At 7:52 a.m. on 20 May 1927, the Spirit bumped down the muddy runway at Roosevelt Field on Long Island and only just cleared the telephone wires at the end. Then came the long, lonely hours. Lindbergh flew over Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and out over the dark Atlantic, through fog and cloud where ice began to coat the wings. The hardest enemy was sleep. He had been awake for more than a day before he even took off, and he later wrote that the plane's twitchy handling, which forced him to keep correcting it, helped keep him awake. After a night over the ocean he sighted fishing boats, then the coast of Ireland, only a few kilometres from where he had aimed.

At 10:22 p.m. Paris time on 21 May, after about 33 and a half hours alone in the air, he landed at Le Bourget airfield. He had imagined a quiet arrival. Instead, roughly 150,000 people poured across the field, lifted him out of the cockpit and carried him around on their shoulders, while souvenir hunters began tearing pieces of fabric off his plane until soldiers and police rescued it.

Lindbergh became the most famous person in the world almost overnight. He won the Orteig Prize, and Time magazine named him its first Man of the Year. Remember, though, that he was not the first to fly the Atlantic; he was the first to fly solo and nonstop between New York and Paris. His real impact came next. He toured 82 American cities in all 48 states, and the excitement became known as the Lindbergh Boom: within months the amount of air mail jumped by about half, applications for pilot licences tripled, and the number of airplanes grew several times over. Ordinary people began to see flying not just as a stunt, but as the future. Later in life Lindbergh's reputation was damaged by his political views before the Second World War, and historians still discuss that side of his story, but nobody doubts the courage of his 1927 flight. The Spirit of St. Louis now hangs in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.

sections.heading: Amelia Earhart: Across the Atlantic and Into Mystery
paragraphs: A year after Lindbergh, in June 1928, a young social worker and pilot from Kansas named Amelia Earhart became the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air, aboard a three-engine plane called Friendship. The journey from Newfoundland to Burry Port in Wales took about 21 hours. But Earhart was a passenger, not a pilot, and she said she felt like a sack of potatoes. Newspapers called her Lady Lindy anyway. She was determined to earn the title properly.

On 20 May 1932, exactly five years after Lindbergh's departure, Earhart took off alone from Harbour Grace, Newfoundland, in a bright red Lockheed Vega 5B. That night her altimeter failed, ice formed on the wings, and flames flickered from a cracked exhaust pipe. Fighting strong winds, she decided not to try for Paris, and after about 15 hours she landed in a cow pasture at Culmore, just north of the city of Derry in Northern Ireland. A surprised farm worker asked if she had flown far, and she reportedly replied that she had come from America. She was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, and only the second person ever to do it.

In 1937, Earhart set out on her biggest adventure: to be the first woman to fly around the world, roughly following the equator. Her plane was a twin-engine Lockheed Electra 10E, and her navigator was Fred Noonan, an experienced navigator of Pan Am's ocean flying boats. After a crash ended their first attempt in Hawaii, they started again, heading east from Miami on 1 June 1937. Hopping across South America, Africa, Asia and Australia, they reached Lae, in New Guinea, at the end of June with about three-quarters of the trip done. The hardest leg was next: about 4,100 kilometres across the Pacific Ocean to Howland Island, a tiny speck of land only about 2 kilometres long. A US Coast Guard ship, the Itasca, waited there to guide them by radio.

They took off on 2 July 1937. Many hours later the radio operators on the Itasca heard Earhart's voice saying she was running low on fuel and could not see the island. The ship could hear her, but for reasons that are still debated, the radio connection never worked well both ways, and the Electra never arrived. The United States Navy and Coast Guard searched a vast area of ocean, often given as about 650,000 square kilometres, for over two weeks, but found nothing.

What happened to Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan is still unknown. The official conclusion was that they probably ran out of fuel and went down in the ocean near Howland. Others think they may have landed on a remote reef island to the south, called Nikumaroro, and expeditions have searched there, but nothing found so far has proved it. Other ideas are even less certain. What we do know is that Earhart inspired generations of pilots, especially women, and that her disappearance showed how much flying across oceans still depended on courage, luck and the tiny radios of the day.

By the late 1930s, people had watched pilots risk everything to fly mail, cross oceans and set records. The newspapers were full of heroes. But in towns and cities around the world, more and more ordinary people were looking up at the sky with a new question in their minds: not who will be the next hero, but could I fly somewhere too?

deepDive: Historians often say that the First World War compressed decades of aviation progress into four years, and the numbers support them. In August 1914 the armies of Europe had only a few hundred usable airplanes between them, mostly unarmed scouts with engines of under 100 horsepower. By 1918 the leading powers were producing aircraft on an industrial scale, fighter engines of 200 to 300 horsepower were common, and air forces had developed specialised roles that still exist: reconnaissance, artillery spotting, fighters, ground attack and strategic bombing. The synchronization gear is a good example of how wartime pressure works. The idea had been patented before the war by Franz Schneider and tried by Raymond Saulnier, whose test failed largely because his Hotchkiss gun fired unevenly. Fokker's team succeeded in 1915 because they had a captured example to study, an urgent military demand and a gun that suited semi-automatic triggering. Historians now treat the old story of Fokker inventing it single-handedly in 48 hours as a myth. Interwar aviation, by contrast, was driven largely by prizes, mail contracts and publicity. The Daily Mail and Orteig prizes encouraged risky record attempts, and several crews died trying before Alcock and Brown and Lindbergh succeeded. Government air mail did something less glamorous but more important: it paid for routes, airfields, weather reports and night lighting, and the 1925 Contract Air Mail Act turned that infrastructure into a business for private airlines. Records also need careful wording. The NC-4 crossed the Atlantic in stages in May 1919, the R34 airship crossed in both directions that July, Alcock and Brown flew it nonstop, and Lindbergh's achievement was the first solo nonstop flight between New York and Paris. Earhart's 1932 flight was the first solo Atlantic crossing by a woman. As for her disappearance in 1937, the evidence is still incomplete: the official conclusion was that she probably ran out of fuel near Howland Island, while the Nikumaroro hypothesis remains unproven despite many expeditions. Good historians keep such questions open until real evidence settles them.
funFact: Because one sheet of the 1918 air mail stamp was printed with its airplane upside down, a single 24-cent Inverted Jenny stamp sold in 2023 for about two million dollars.

check.q: What was special about Charles Lindbergh's 1927 flight to Paris?
check.a: It was the first solo nonstop flight from New York to Paris.
wrong: It was the first flight of any kind across the Atlantic.
It was the first flight to carry passengers to Europe.
It was the first flight to use a jet engine.
